newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS-Gilt, short stg vols steady before budget.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS-Gilt, short stg vols steady before budget.

text.p: Implied volatility of gilt and short sterling options was steady to firmer on Wednesday as dealers awaited the outcome of the first budget from Britain's new Labour government.

"The main options trade will be tomorrow - no one can really trade while they are waiting for this," said one options broker on the LIFFE floor, referring to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's budget speech due to begin at 1430 GMT.
Gilt options volatility was slightly firmer quoted by one floor broker at 6.5 to 7.1 percent for August, 6.8 to 7.1 pct for September and 6.5 to 7.1 pct for December.
LIFFE data showed closing levels on Tuesday of 6.45 percent for August, 6.71 percent for September and 6.74 percent for December.
September gilt futures were trading at 114-27 at 1100 GMT, up 7/32 on the day.
The market was uncertain about the contents of the budget speech, options traders said.
The FTSE share index rallied on Tuesday on rumours that the government would keep a credit on ACT (Advanced Corporation Tax) which provides an effective tax relief for pension funds.
"They have got to abolish ACT, they've prepared the markets for it," said one options broker for a British firm. "The recent rally was overdone."
Options dealers were also looking for a cut in housing relief and for an eventual rise in British interest rates when the Bank of England's policy committee meets on July 9 and 10.
"Short sterling is pricing it in," said one options broker at a U.S. brokerage.

September short sterling was up 0.03 at 92.96 implying money market rates of 7.04 percent against official rates of 6.5 percent while December short sterling was at 92.80 discounting rates of 7.20 percent.
Implied volatility of short sterling options was steady at 8.2 to 9.2 percent for September, 8.7 to 9.6 percent for December and 10.0 to 10.5 percent for March 1998, dealers said.

Put buyers were active in short sterling, particularly in the 92.75 strike where two large houses executed one-by-two put spreads, dealers said. A total of 3,000 lots had changed hands in that strike by 1100 GMT.
A response to the budget would be limited on Wednesday, as gilt and short sterling options do not trade on APT (automated pit trade), the LIFFE after hours trading system.
On Wednesday, floor trading for gilts futures and options will end at 1515 GMT as usual but floor trading for short sterling futures and options will be extended to 1515 from 1505 GMT.

Double uncertainty in the form of the British budget and a statement on U.S. interest rates from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) expected at around 1815 GMT was keeping some market participants away.
"A couple of the big locals haven't bothered to turn up today," said one broker from a British firm. "They've locked in their money and they'll be here again tomorrow morning."
